name: Danish Gold Coast
alt: Danish West India and Guinea Company Gold Coast
Danish possessions on the Gold Coast

predecessors.name: Swedish Empire
predecessors.text: Fort Carlsborg at Cape Coast and Fort Christiansborg at Osu, the Swedish forts seized in 1658

successors.name: British Colonial Empire
successors.text: all Danish forts and settlements, sold to Britain on 30 March 1850

ledger.x: 1658: Carloff seizes the Swedish forts on the Gold Coast for Denmark.
1659: Commander Schmidt abandons Fort Carlsborg and sells it and the Danish stations to the Dutch.
1659: the Danes get Fort Frederiksborg at Cape Coast.
1660: Fort Christiansborg passes to the Dutch.
1679-80: a mutiny at Christiansborg and the sale to the Portuguese.
1685: the English buy Fort Frederiksborg outright ('The English bought the fort outright, so the Danes lost it through sale'; pawned to the English in 1679; the Danish forts table: ceded 1685).
1685: the Danish Gold Coast's capital moves from Fort Frederiksborg to Fort Christiansborg at Osu.
1734: the Danes found Fort Fredensborg at Old Ningo.
1744: Cliopatria's Danish shape falls from 1,349 to 718 km2; Fort Fredensborg's cell at Old Ningo stays.
1784: Forts Prinsensten (Keta) and Kongensten (Ada) are founded.
1787: Fort Augustaborg is founded at Teshie.
1850: Denmark sells its Gold Coast to Britain.

wars.name: Danish capture of the Swedish Gold Coast
wars.outcome: Carloff, with a Danish letter of marque of August 1657, sailed in December 1657, reached the Gold Coast in January 1658 and captured all the Swedish forts in February 1658; the Swedes demanded their return under the Treaty of Roskilde and the Treaty of…

wars.name: Dutch-Danish-Swedish contest for Carlsborg
wars.outcome: Carlsborg changed hands several times: sold to the Dutch (1659), retaken by Classen of Fetu, handed to the Swedish Africa Company (10 December 1660), retaken by the Dutch (1663), taken by the English fleet under Holmes with Danish help (May 1664) and renamed…

wars.name: Akwamu occupation of Christiansborg
wars.outcome: The Akwamu occupied the fort in 1693 and sold it back to Denmark-Norway in 1694 for 50 marks of gold, keeping the keys.
